what: verses, images and doctrines of the self, Brahman and the paths after death
era: Upaniṣadic period to the Gītā's composition

evidence.detail: the chapter colophons call the Gītā an upaniṣad; the Gītādhyāna calls it the milk drawn by Kṛṣṇa from the Upaniṣads as cows

what: the sacrificial frame, reinterpreted as action without attachment, inner offerings and the sacrifice of knowledge

evidence.detail: the wheel of sacrifice (BhG 3.10–16); the many sacrifices (4.25–30); the Anugītā's seven priests (14.20)

what: enumeration of principles and the discrimination of puruṣa from prakṛti

evidence.detail: the Mokṣadharma names Kapila, Āsuri and Pañcaśikha, the same founders the classical tradition names
epic Sāṃkhya (with its 24/25/26 counts and a Lord) is often held to precede Īśvarakṛṣṇa's non-theistic system; the tradition instead sees the epic as reporting an already existing Sāṃkhya

what: yoga vocabulary: practice and dispassion, concentration (dhāraṇā), yoga-power, the faults of yoga, the first meditation with vitarka and vicāra
era: scholarly: epic and early classical period

evidence.detail: BhG 6.35 (abhyāsa and vairāgya) ~ YS 1.12; MBh 12.188.15 (vicāra, vitarka) ~ YS 1.17; MBh 12.289 (dhāraṇā, yogabala)

what: the fourfold form (vyūha) doctrine and Sātvata worship of Vāsudeva
era: scholarly: c. 1st c. BCE – 5th c. CE

evidence.detail: the Nārāyaṇīya calls its teaching 'Pañcarātra' (12.326.100) and names the fourfold form (12.326.68–69)
the Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās trace their teaching to Nārāyaṇa's revelation

what: the Lord's manifestations and Kṛṣṇa devotion

evidence.detail: the Nārāyaṇīya's list of manifestations (12.326.72–94) and BhG 4.7–8 prefigure the Purāṇic avatāra lists; the Harivaṃśa's life of Kṛṣṇa is continued in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas

what: the Bhagavad Gītā as one of the three canonical sources (prasthānatraya)

evidence.detail: every Vedānta school comments on the Gītā (Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, Madhva, Nimbārka school, Vallabha school, Gauḍīya)

what: the vocabulary of the first meditation (vitarka, vicāra, viveka) and of nirvāṇa

evidence.detail: MBh 12.188.15 names vicāra, vitarka and viveka as arising in 'the first dhyāna', close to the Pali first jhāna formula; the Gītā speaks of brahmanirvāṇa and 'the peace that culminates in nirvāṇa' (6.15)
some scholars see Buddhist influence on the epic here, others common ascetic vocabulary; the direction is disputed and each tradition defines its own terms

what: shared didactic narratives: the father–son dialogue on renunciation and the parable of the man in the well

evidence.detail: MBh 12.169 (the son urging his father to renounce) parallels Uttarādhyayana 14; the parable of the man hanging over a well (MBh 11.5–6) recurs in Jain story literature

what: a doctrine of six colours of living beings

evidence.detail: the Vṛtra Gītā's six colours of beings (MBh 12.271.33) resemble the Ājīvika six classes (abhijāti), reported in Buddhist texts, and the Jain six leśyās
